title: Company Field Measurements: Lessons Learned

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Exterior parking lot pole at mid-morning; bucket truck parked beside it, cones set. Matthew in a company polo, medium shot, meter in hand.
scenes.on_screen: Job Mindset: Measure Before You Connect
scenes.says: Before you take a single reading today, picture the job. The hazard is exposed energized conductors, so the top control is to work it dead whenever you can. When you can't, only a qualified person measures, in the right PPE, with a verified meter. Plan before you leave the shop: meter, test leads, PPE, the right voltage driver, and a backup plan if the voltage surprises you.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Same pole. Lower third: Matthew Berrett, Program Lead. Cut to close-up of a CAT-rated meter being checked on a known live source at the truck.
scenes.on_screen: Energized readings = qualified + PPE + verified meter
scenes.says: Here's the safety rule for this whole lesson. Every voltage reading on an exposed energized circuit is energized work under NFPA 70E. Only qualified persons take these readings, with the PPE your company program requires, using a CAT-rated meter you've checked on a known source. And scope varies by state and city. Confirm with your supervisor that you're allowed and authorized in that location. When in doubt, stop and ask.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech in required PPE at the opened pole handhole measures the existing supply; presenter voice-over. Close-ups of the meter display.
scenes.on_screen: L-N  |  L-L  |  L-G | Qualified persons only
scenes.says: Measurement one. Our company has destroyed many brand-new LED fixtures on power-up because someone assumed the voltage. So on every exterior project, and any replacement you didn't install originally, measure first. Hot to neutral tells you 120, 277, or in some places 347. Hot to hot tells you 208, 240 or 480. Hot to ground confirms the grounding path. Check live voltage only once your supervisor has deemed you qualified for this task, wearing the required PPE, with a CAT-rated meter verified live-dead-live.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up: new fixture label reading 120-277 V held next to the meter showing 480 V. Senior tech writes on a work order clipboard.
scenes.says: Now compare with the new fixture's label. A 120 to 277 volt driver connected to 480 is destroyed the instant power comes on. If it's fed hot to hot at 480, you need a 480-rated driver or a step-down transformer, so stop and call your supervisor. Then write it down: measured 277 volts hot to neutral at pole 4. That's how the office quotes the right replacement.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Office ceiling with a dark 2x4 LED troffer; ladder set, door open. Senior tech, qualified and in PPE, places meter leads at the driver input; presenter voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Step 1 on a dark LED: meter across hot and neutral | Qualified persons only
scenes.says: Measurement two. Ask any of our supervisors what Step 1 is on a dark LED fixture, and you'll hear the same thing: put your meter across the hot and the neutral. Not a sniffer. A non-contact tester warns, it doesn't measure. It can't tell 120 from 277, and it can be fooled by induced voltage or shielding.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Same troffer. Senior tech applies a lock and tag at the panel, then performs live-dead-live at the fixture. Split screen with a simple decision graphic.
scenes.on_screen: No voltage = upstream problem. Don't replace the driver.
scenes.says: Read the result. No voltage at the fixture? The fault is upstream: breaker, switch, sensor, photocell, contactor, a loose splice or an open neutral. A new driver won't fix it. Voltage hot to ground but not hot to neutral? Suspect an open neutral. Correct voltage present? Now lock out, verify dead live-dead-live, and move on to the driver and the LED boards.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Lift truck in the shop yard, boom stowed. Senior tech checks the fuse panel, then sets a DMM to DC volts at the 24 V boom battery bank; presenter voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Boom won't raise: fuses, then 24 V minimum on the bank
scenes.says: Measurement three is on the truck. A boom that won't raise or lower while every other function works? On trucks with a 24 volt boom battery bank, suspect low batteries. Call the equipment service line and check fuses and relays first. Then DC volts across the whole bank. 24 volts is the minimum. Then measure each battery separately, because one weak battery drags the whole bank down.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up: tech removes ring and watch, puts on safety glasses, uses insulated tools. Then unplugs a charger by the plug and presses RESET on a GFCI outlet.
scenes.on_screen: Rings off. Insulated tools. Eye protection.
scenes.says: Battery banks can deliver very high current. Remove rings and watches, use insulated tools, wear eye protection, and never lay a tool across the terminals. Check the charging system the manufacturer's way. If you just need to stow the boom, the manufacturer's emergency lowering procedure comes first. And chargers are fragile. Unplug them by the plug, and if the charge light's off, check and reset the GFCI first.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Back at the parking lot pole, Matthew to camera, medium close-up.
scenes.says: The meter only works if it's with you and turned on. Check it on a known live source, and record every reading with the location and conditions. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Three field segments per the lesson's video suggestion. Performer for all energized readings must be a qualified tech in the PPE the company program requires; show CAT rating on the meter. Show live-dead-live at the troffer before any driver work. Lift-truck segment: use a truck with a 24 V boom battery bank; demonstrate PPE (eye protection, rings and watch removed, insulated tools). No customer logos at the pole or office.
